subtitle: An independent review of how the website performs for a first-time, full-fee patient — what it does well, and where attention is lost before a consultation is booked.
summary: KORA has something most practices in this market cannot claim: founder-led by a national clinical trainer. That is a genuine differentiator, and the site offers three separate routes to contact — “Book Now” in the header, “Claim Your Free Consultation” in the hero, and a sticky contact bar on mobile. The commercial machinery is in better shape than almost every site we have reviewed.

The opportunity is that the headline is written for a search engine rather than a patient. “Medical Spa in Scottsdale, AZ & Paradise Valley | Founder-Led by a National Clinical Trainer” is a page title — fifteen words with a pipe separator down the middle — occupying the position where a patient decides whether to keep reading. And the trainer is never named, so the strongest claim on the page has no person attached to it.

Evidence limitation: this review covers the homepage on mobile plus publicly visible information. Treatment-page depth and technical performance were not assessed, so the score is normalised across the six categories that were. Nothing here uses private analytics, and no traffic or revenue figures have been estimated.
scoreNote: Normalised across six assessed categories (90 points available). Treatment content and technical performance were not reviewed and are excluded rather than guessed. This is the strongest site in our current batch — the recommendations are about getting full value from assets already in place.

scorecard.finding: The headline is a page title, complete with a pipe separator.
A national clinical trainer — who is never named.
Three routes to contact, including a sticky mobile bar.
Clear actions; no proof sitting beside any of them.
An accessibility widget overlaps the body copy.
Both service areas named in the headline itself.

strengthsLead: This site does more right than most. The recommendations below are refinements, not repairs.

strengths.title: Founder-led by a national clinical trainer.
strengths.body: A practitioner who trains other practitioners is close to the strongest authority signal available in aesthetics. Very few practices can say it, and it is already on the first screen.

strengths.title: Three routes to contact, all obvious.
strengths.body: “Book Now” in the header, “Claim Your Free Consultation” in the hero, and a sticky Contact Us and call bar fixed to the foot of the mobile screen. A patient can act from anywhere on the page.

strengths.title: The consultation is free.
strengths.body: Removing the cost of the first step is the single most effective way to lower the barrier for a patient who is interested but not yet committed.

strengths.title: Both service areas are named up front.
strengths.body: Scottsdale and Paradise Valley both appear in the largest text on the page — correct for two-area local search, and many practices name only one.

captionDesktop: Desktop, 1366×768. The hero is a background video of the practice signage. The video player's own title — “Kora Aesthetics / tourhazara” — and a pause control are showing through over it.
captionMobile: Mobile, 390×844. A fifteen-word headline with a pipe separator, an outlined consultation button, and a sticky Contact Us bar at the foot.

findings.heading: The headline is a page title, not a headline.
findings.evidence: The hero reads “Medical Spa in Scottsdale, AZ & Paradise Valley | Founder-Led by a National Clinical Trainer” — fifteen words containing a vertical pipe separator, the convention used in browser tab titles and search results.
findings.why: It is doing a search engine's job in a patient's space. A pipe in the middle of a sentence tells a reader nothing, and by the time they reach the genuinely persuasive part — founder-led by a national clinical trainer — they have waded through a location list first.
findings.recommended: Keep the full version as the page's title tag, where it earns its keep, and give the visible headline the differentiator alone. “Founder-led by a national clinical trainer” is a strong opening line by itself.

findings.heading: The national clinical trainer is never named.
findings.evidence: The homepage states the practice is founder-led by a national clinical trainer. No name, qualification or photograph accompanies the claim on the first screen.
findings.why: An unnamed authority is a claim; a named one is evidence. A patient deciding who should hold the needle wants a person, a credential and a face — and here the practice has all three and is publishing none of them at the point of decision.
findings.recommended: Name her, state the qualification, and put a real photograph beside it in the hero. This is the single highest-value change on this list and it requires no redesign.

findings.heading: Search phrases appear inside the body copy.
findings.evidence: The paragraph below the hero includes the phrase “best med spa near me” set in bold within the sentence.
findings.why: “Near me” is how someone types into Google, not how anyone speaks. A reader notices the seam, and it makes the surrounding sentences read as written for a machine — which quietly undermines the credibility the credential above it was building.
findings.recommended: Write the sentence as you would say it to a patient in the room. Search engines have long since stopped needing the phrase repeated verbatim, and a human reader still notices when it is.

findings.heading: The hero button is quieter than the header button.
findings.evidence: “Claim Your Free Consultation” is set as white text in a thin white outline over a photograph, while “Book Now” in the header is a solid black block.
findings.why: The more valuable offer — a free consultation — is presented more faintly than the smaller one above it. Outlined controls over photographs are frequently read as decoration rather than as something to press.
findings.recommended: Give the hero button a solid fill so it outweighs the header button. It is the better offer and should look like it.

findings.heading: The video player's own labels are showing through the hero.
findings.evidence: On desktop the hero plays a background video of the practice signage. Over it, at the top left, the words “Kora Aesthetics” and “tourhazara” appear in the player's own typeface, with a pause control in the centre of the frame.
findings.why: That text is the video file's title and uploader, not anything the practice wrote. It reads as leftover scaffolding — the sort of detail a visitor cannot name but registers as unfinished, on the very screen where the practice is establishing that it is precise and clinical.
findings.recommended: Turn off the player's title and controls in the embed settings, or host the clip as a plain background video with no player chrome. The footage itself is good and worth showing cleanly.

findings.heading: An accessibility widget sits on top of the copy.
findings.evidence: At 390×844 a circular accessibility control is fixed to the lower left of the screen and overlaps the opening words of the paragraph beneath the hero.
findings.why: The widget is there for good reasons, but as positioned it obscures the first words of the first paragraph a visitor reads — so the tool intended to improve access is reducing it.
findings.recommended: Move it clear of the text column, or dock it to the same bar as the contact controls so all the floating elements share one edge.

psychology.plain: People expect a site to behave like the others they use.
psychology.site: Strong. Menu, search, Book Now — everything sits where a visitor expects to find it.

psychology.plain: Important actions should be big and easy to thumb.
psychology.site: Excellent. A sticky contact bar keeps Contact Us and the phone within thumb reach throughout.

psychology.plain: Reassurance has to sit where the doubt is.
psychology.site: No review, rating or named credential appears beside any of the three contact actions.
The strongest claim on the page — national clinical trainer — has no name, face or qualification attached to it.
Three routes to contact could compete, but they resolve to the same outcome, so the effect is helpful rather than confusing.

psychology.plain: Sensible pre-selections that serve the patient.
psychology.site: A free consultation is the most helpful default available: it makes the first step cost nothing.

psychology.plain: Balanced, realistic communication is trusted more than perfection.
psychology.site: “Best med spa near me” in the body copy is the least believable line on an otherwise credible page.

roadmap.actions: Name the founder with her qualification and photograph in the hero. Shorten the visible headline and keep the long version as the title tag. Give the consultation button a solid fill. Move the accessibility widget clear of the text.
Add a rating and review count beside the consultation button. Rewrite the search phrases in the body copy as spoken sentences. Add treatment-specific reassurance on the highest-value pages.

Build authority content around the training credential — it is a genuine differentiator and currently under-used. Post-treatment review requests. Begin measuring enquiry-to-booking so the calculator figures above become yours.

limitations: This review assessed the homepage at 390 pixels wide together with publicly visible information. Treatment-page depth and technical performance were not assessed and are excluded from the score rather than estimated; the total is normalised across the six categories reviewed (90 points available).
